issues.title: Missing conditioning in the unbiased-estimator extension

failure_location.quote: Note, the discussed results remain valid if the stochastic gradient $\nabla f_{i_k}$ is replaced by any unbiased gradient estimator $g_k$ satisfying $\mathbb{E}[g_k]=\nabla f(\theta_k)$.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Taking the conditional expectation given $\theta_k$ yields

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that all discussed results extend to any g_k satisfying the printed unconditional equality E[g_k]=grad f(theta_k). The old proofs actually replace the random direction after conditioning on theta_k, which requires E[g_k | theta_k]=grad f(theta_k). An unconditional mean does not supply that identity when g_k is correlated with the iterate or its history, so the stated extension exceeds what the argument supports.
issues.overall_effect: The original theorems for uniformly sampled component gradients remain unaffected, but the prose extension to arbitrary stochastic estimators is not justified as printed.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the extension's hypothesis by conditional unbiasedness, $\mathbb{E}[g_k\mid\theta_k]=\nabla f(\theta_k)$, and invoke the existing conditional-expectation arguments under that condition. The original results for uniformly sampled component gradients require no change.
issues.why_classification: The unconditional condition is insufficient for the proof, so this is not purely transcriptional. Conditional unbiasedness is the standard, local stochastic-dependence qualification already exhibited by the source; adding it preserves the method, conclusions, rates, and intended estimator regime without affecting the original theorems.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: Note, the discussed results remain valid if the stochastic gradient $\nabla f_{i_k}$ is replaced by any unbiased gradient estimator $g_k$ satisfying $\mathbb{E}[g_k\mid \theta_k]=\nabla f(\theta_k)$.

issues.title: Missing modulus in the smoothness definition
issues.failure_explanation: The primary theorem assumes hp_smooth and restricts its step size using L_max. Under the printed definition, L is unused, so only a unit-Lipschitz gradient is defined and the expression L_i-smooth has no parameterized meaning supplied by the paper. Thus L_max is not tied to the actual component smoothness needed by the theorem, and the same invalid interface affects the later SGD theorems.
issues.overall_effect: All four SGD convergence results invoke smoothness constants whose intended mathematical meaning is not established by the printed definition.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Define $L$-smoothness by $\|\nabla f(\theta_1)-\nabla f(\theta_2)\|\leq L\|\theta_1-\theta_2\|$. Retain the $L_i$-smooth assumptions and all four $L_{\max}$-based convergence results under this corrected definition.
issues.why_classification: The old definition introduces $L>0$, immediately uses the parameterized phrase "$L_i$-smooth," and bases every affected step-size restriction on those constants. These features uniquely force the missing factor $L$; inserting it repairs no inference and changes none of the affected guarantees.

issues.title: Wrong component range in L_max
issues.failure_explanation: The primary theorem uses L_max to restrict the SGD step size, but hp_smooth defines it using the unrelated parameter dimension n. When n>m the maximum contains undefined constants; when n<m it does not control all sampled component gradients. Hence the theorem's step-size hypothesis is not uniformly meaningful for the finite-sum problem, and the same defect reaches every later theorem using L_max.
issues.overall_effect: The step-size restrictions and constants in all four SGD convergence results may be undefined or fail to control every component function.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace $L_{\max}:=\max_{i=1,\ldots,n}L_i$ by $L_{\max}:=\max_{i=1,\ldots,m}L_i$ in Assumption hp_smooth. The existing downstream step-size restrictions and constants can then remain unchanged.
issues.why_classification: The old source defines exactly $m$ component functions and their constants, while $n$ is the unrelated parameter dimension. Thus the range $1,\ldots,m$ is uniquely forced, and the proof reasoning already requires the maximum over all sampled components; this is an index transcription error despite its repeated downstream use.

issues.title: Categorical nonconvergence overclaim for constant-step SGD

failure_location.quote: This result tells us that SGD does not converge with a constant step size.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: If the variance of the gradient estimate was zero

issues.failure_explanation: The prose claims that constant-step SGD does not converge. The preceding theorem actually establishes only an upper bound consisting of a decaying term plus a constant variance term; an upper bound that does not tend to zero is not a lower bound and cannot prove nonconvergence. Moreover, the old discussion explicitly says that the zero-variance admissible case converges. The supported conclusion is therefore only that this result does not guarantee convergence under a constant step size.
issues.overall_effect: The prose materially overstates the behavioral consequence of the strongly convex convergence bound, while the formal theorem itself is not defeated by this root.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the categorical sentence by: “For $\sigma^2>0$, this estimate does not guarantee convergence of constant-step SGD to the solution, because its upper bound contains a nonvanishing variance term.” Retain the subsequent observation that the zero-variance case has linear convergence.
issues.why_classification: An upper bound with a nonzero limiting term cannot establish actual nonconvergence, and the source itself supplies a convergent admissible case. Repair therefore necessarily retracts the categorical behavioral claim. The weakening is mathematically meaningful but limited: a closely comparable interpretation of the same bound survives locally, and no formal theorem or proof architecture changes.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: This result tells us that SGD is not guaranteed to converge with a constant step size, since the upper bound on the error does not go to zero when $k$ increases.

issues.title: Malformed stationarity quantity in the nonconvex theorem
issues.failure_explanation: The theorem assumes the SGD sequence theta_k but states a minimum of an expression involving only bar-theta_K, making the minimum algebraically vacuous. The earlier definitions of bar-theta_K occur inside convex theorems with different hypotheses and step-size rules, so they do not supply the missing nonconvex construction. The theorem consequently fails to state a well-defined iterate-wise stationarity guarantee.
issues.overall_effect: Both the principal stationarity estimate and its epsilon-complexity consequence refer to the wrong or undefined iterate quantity.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: In both the principal stationarity estimate and its $\epsilon$-complexity consequence, replace the quantity under the minimum by $\mathbb{E}[\|\nabla f(\theta_k)\|^2]$, yielding $\min_{k=0,\ldots,K-1}\mathbb{E}[\|\nabla f(\theta_k)\|^2]$. No averaged-iterate construction is needed.
issues.why_classification: The explicit minimum over $k$ and the theorem's only applicable iterate sequence uniquely force evaluation at $\theta_k$. The printed $\bar\theta_K$ is independent of $k$ and has no definition under the nonconvex hypotheses. Replacing this copied symbol restores the intended iterate-wise guarantee and its rate without repairing an inference or supplying a new argument.

issues.title: Undefined L_f in the nonconvex theorem
issues.failure_explanation: Assumption hp_smooth introduces only the component constants L_i and L_max. The additional L_f in the theorem is never bound to a property of f, so the prescribed step size and right-hand-side constant cannot be instantiated from the stated hypotheses. Since the average objective has a Lipschitz gradient under hp_smooth, the missing binding can be supplied locally.
issues.overall_effect: The nonconvex theorem's step size and numerical convergence constant are undefined as printed.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add that $L_f$ denotes a Lipschitz constant of $\nabla f$. Assumption hp_smooth guarantees such a constant; for example, $L_f=(1/m)\sum_{i=1}^m L_i$ is valid. Use this binding in the stated step size and convergence constant without otherwise changing the theorem or its complexity consequence.
issues.why_classification: The undefined parameter prevents the theorem from being instantiated, but its existence follows by a routine one-line smoothness calculation from the component assumptions. Supplying and checking that derived binding is genuine mathematical interface work rather than a uniquely forced transcription edit, yet it is entirely local and preserves the hypotheses, conclusion, rate, and complexity.

new_version_repair_locator.quote: where $L_f$ is the Lipschitz constant of the gradient of $f$.

issues.title: Undefined starred heterogeneity term
issues.failure_explanation: The convergence bound contains Delta_f^star, but the theorem supplies a definition only for Delta_f. Consequently the constant in the bound is undefined. The adjacent definition uniquely identifies the intended heterogeneity quantity, so the mismatch is independently checkable without reconstructing an external theorem.
issues.overall_effect: The numerical constant in the nonconvex stationarity bound, and hence the stated bound itself, cannot be evaluated as printed.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace $\Delta_f^{\star}$ in the stationarity bound by the adjacent defined quantity $\Delta_f:=\inf f-(1/m)\sum_{i=1}^m\inf f_i$, making the notation consistent throughout the theorem.
issues.why_classification: The adjacent definition uniquely fixes the heterogeneity quantity used by the bound, and no distinct starred quantity is introduced or needed. Making the two labels agree is a purely transcriptional correction that changes neither the numerical constant nor any mathematical reasoning.
